p: The aviation medical examiner in Englewood worked out of a second floor office above a dentist, and the whole waiting room smelled faintly of mint and drill.

Jordan had filled out the MedXPress form the way she filled out a patient care report, every box, nothing rounded off. The doctor read it with his glasses pushed up on his forehead, listened to her heart for longer than she thought he needed to, and asked how she was sleeping. She told him the truth. Four hours, five on a good night, since March. He wrote something down, asked two more questions, and then asked a third that wasn't on any form: was she planning to fly tired. She said no. He looked at her the way she looked at drunk drivers who said they'd only had two, and then he signed.
FAA medical certificate, third class. Name: JORDAN E. REYES. Class: THIRD. Limitations: NONE. This certificate shall be valid for the period prescribed in 14 CFR 61.23.

It was a piece of paper the size of an index card. She'd expected to feel something about it. Mostly she felt the same thing she'd felt in April, when the whole family had gone in for heart screening because that's what you do after a sudden cardiac arrest at 41. Echo, ECG, a cardiologist with cold hands who said "normal" like he was handing her a present. She'd driven home from that one and sat in the driveway for twenty minutes. This time she just put the card in her wallet behind her driver's license and went to get a burrito.
Her phone buzzed in the parking lot. Another number she didn't have saved. She was starting to think the airport had a phone tree.

A text from Marisol Tran. This is Marisol. I do the wrenching on Biscuit. Abby says you read the whole checklist. Saturday 8am, hangar six. Cowling's coming off for an oil change. Wear clothes you hate.

Jordan read it in the car. She knew the name. Danny had said it a few hundred times over the years, usually as a verdict. Marisol says it's fine. Marisol says absolutely not. At the funeral a woman with short gray streaked hair and a work jacket had stood at the very back, left before the reception, and sent flowers with a card that said only BISCUIT MISSES YOU TOO.
She texted back: I'll be there. Then, after a minute: I don't own clothes I hate. I'll wear work pants.
The reply came instantly. You'll hate them by noon.

Hangar Six was the sixth door in a long row of corrugated steel hangars on the north side of the field, and inside it Biscuit sat with her nose naked. The cowling lay on a moving blanket like a shell somebody had cracked open. Under it the engine was smaller than Jordan expected, four fat finned cylinders laid flat, two on each side, wires and tubes everywhere like the inside of a ten year old's model kit.

Marisol was on a rolling stool with a drain pan and did not get up. She was shorter than Jordan, with forearms like rope and a pencil behind each ear. A radio on the workbench was playing classic rock, volume at about two. On the back wall of the hangar was a whiteboard, half covered in block capitals Jordan knew from a lifetime of birthday cards. DUE LIST. ANNUAL AUGUST 2026. TRANSPONDER OCTOBER 2026. ELT BATTERY MARCH 2026. It hadn't been touched in a while. There was a calendar next to it from a parts supplier, still on March. A coffee can of spare fuel caps sat on the shelf under the board.
You're Jordan. Not a question. Okay. Lesson one. Go turn the prop for me, slowly, so you can feel the compression in each cylinder. She went back to the oil filter.

Marisol stops wiping her hands on the rag. Mags off. Key's up on the glare shield. I checked both P leads before you got here, and I'll still yell if you put an arm through that arc. A pause. Who taught you that? YouTube. Also a guy on B shift named Hector, who has nine fingers and tells everybody why. Marisol almost smiles. Jordan stands off to the side and walks the blade around a few inches at a time, and the cylinders push back against her palm one after another, slow and stubborn, twice every turn.

Marisol pulled the air box off the bottom of the engine and handed Jordan the carburetor's guts to look at, more or less. A throat, a float bowl, a butterfly valve on a shaft. Air comes up through here and speeds up, pressure drops, fuel sprays in and evaporates. Same thing as an aerosol can getting cold in your hand. It can drop the temperature in there forty, fifty, sixty degrees.

She tapped the butterfly valve with a screwdriver. Ice grows right here. Your brother found that out the hard way, once. Ask him about it. She heard what she'd said a second after she said it. The screwdriver stopped moving. Then she cleared her throat. So. Quiz. Which day do you worry about this most?

Marisol points the screwdriver at her. That one. Every pilot thinks ice means winter. It's sixty degrees and wet, throttle mostly closed, engine cooling off. That's when it grows and you don't notice till you push the throttle in and nothing happens.

Marisol had all eight spark plugs out in a tray with numbered holes, a habit, she said, from a guy who once put them back in the wrong cylinders and spent an afternoon learning humility. She held one up to the light. The business end was crusted black and dry, like a match somebody blew out.
This one's from the bottom of number three. Tell me why it looks like that.
Jordan thought about the discovery flight. Abby taxiing out, the long wait behind a Cirrus at the runup area, the mixture knob all the way in the whole time because nobody told her to touch it.

Yep. Carburetor thinks it's at sea level. It isn't. Lean it for taxi, lean it for the runup, and do what the POH says before takeoff up here. She drops the plug in the cleaner. Danny never leaned for taxi. I'd find these every oil change and yell at him, and he'd bring me a coffee, and we'd do it again.
Marisol sent her to walk the airplane while the oil drained. Everything you looked at Saturday with Abby, look at again. I'll know if you didn't.

Under the left wing, behind the strut, the little bent fuel vent tube hung down like a soda straw. Jordan crouched to look up into it. It was packed with something gray and papery. When she tapped it, a wasp walked out, looked at her, and flew away unbothered.

Marisol crouches beside her, looks up the tube, and swears quietly in two languages. She clears it with a wire and blows air through until Jordan, standing at the fuel cap, can hear it whistle. That's the third one this spring. They love this airplane. She writes it on a squawk sheet. Then she writes the date.

By ten thirty the new oil was in and Marisol was safety wiring the oil filter. She finished it, looked at it for a while, snipped it off with a pair of dikes, and started over. The first one had looked perfect to Jordan, a tight little braid. She kept that to herself. Out on the ramp a fuel truck backed up with that beeping that never stops. Somebody out there was trying to start a Cherokee and it wasn't going well.

Next quiz, since you're just standing there. Night flight, you're over Limon on the way home, and the ammeter needle slides left of center and sits there, a steady discharge. What's happening, and what do you do?
She didn't look up from the wire. Jordan was getting the idea that this was what Marisol sounded like when she liked you.

Yep. Engine doesn't care, the mags have it. Radios and lights care a lot. Landing light off, second radio off, call Denver while you can still talk to them, and go find a runway before that battery's dead.

Marisol had washed Biscuit on Friday, which explained why she was the cleanest thing in the hangar. On her second lap around the airplane, Jordan found a square of blue painter's tape stuck neatly over the static port on the side of the fuselage, a little hole she'd only learned the name of a week ago.
Good. I tape it when I wash. Takes it off before anybody flies. She said it with complete confidence. Then she added, more quietly, Usually.
Say it stayed on. You take off. What do the instruments do?
That's it. Altimeter stuck at field elevation. VSI dead flat. Airspeed reading low as you climb, because the trapped pressure behind it is higher than outside.

At noon they ate gas station sandwiches on overturned buckets. The square of blue tape from the static port was stuck to Jordan's kneeboard now. Marisol had peeled it off and pressed it there herself. Keep that. It's a good reminder. Jordan asked where the maintenance logbooks were.

Marisol pointed her sandwich at a fireproof file box on the workbench. Airframe, engine, prop. Fifty years of other people's handwriting. Everything that matters is on the board. She meant Danny's whiteboard. Nobody reads those cover to cover. Owners never do.

At work, Jordan read every line of every run report she signed, including the ones she wrote, because the time you skim is the time a dose is wrong. She looked at the box. She looked at the board, which hadn't been touched since March.

Knock yourself out. Jordan opens a legal pad and starts with the most recent annual, then works backward, one line at a time: date, tach time, what was done, who signed. Marisol goes back to the airplane, then comes back to look over her shoulder twice, pretending to need a wrench from the bench.

It took her an hour and forty minutes. The annual: August 14 last year, signed by Marisol with her IA number. The transponder and static system checks: October two years ago, at the avionics shop on the south side. The ELT inspection: done with the annual. All of it matched the board.

Then a three year old entry for an ELT battery replacement, with a line at the end in Marisol's neat capitals: NEW BATTERY EXPIRATION MARCH 2026. Jordan got up, walked to the tail, and opened the access panel where Marisol had shown her the ELT that morning. The label on the side of the transmitter said the same thing. REPLACE BATTERY MARCH 2026. It had been on the board all morning, too. ELT BATTERY MARCH 2026. She'd read it at eight and walked right past it.
It was May. Danny had died in March. Out in the hangar, Marisol was singing along to a classic rock station, badly, and fixing the fuel selector detent for the second time that day.

Marisol reads the logbook line. Then the label. Then the logbook line again. She doesn't say anything for long enough that the song on the radio ends. Then she says, very calmly, I wrote that. I wrote it right there in my own handwriting, and I told him to put it on the board, and he did. She sets the logbook down too carefully. And then I stopped looking at the board, because he always looked at the board.

Marisol was on the phone with the parts counter at the shop across the field within two minutes. They'd have a battery Monday. She hung up and kicked the rolling stool across the hangar, not hard, and then went and got it and sat on it.
Russ flew it to Steamboat in April. Over the Divide. With a dead ELT battery, and I'm the one who should've caught it. She wasn't talking to Jordan, exactly.
Jordan had a lesson with Abby on Tuesday morning. Her shifts didn't move. She asked the only question she had.
By then Marisol had put it in the partners' chat. Russ answered first.
A message from Russ Kim. wait. i flew it over the divide last month. with an expired elt battery. cool. cool cool cool. marisol i'm buying you a beer and also never flying again

Marisol nods once. Monday. I'll swap it, run the test, mark the new date on the case and in the book. You fly Tuesday. She stands up, walks to the whiteboard, and draws a box around the ELT battery line without erasing it.

Walt came by at three, as promised, for the first of his monthly logbook checks. He read Jordan's pilot logbook, all 0.9 hours of it, with his glasses on the end of his nose, initialed the bottom of the page, and then listened to Marisol tell him about the ELT battery without interrupting once.

When she finished he said, That's on all four of us. Then he picked up Jordan's legal pad and read her due list. At the bottom she'd written: 100 HOUR, DUE AT TACH 2,441.8? WHY? She'd circled WHY twice.
Go ahead, he said. Tell me why you think Biscuit gets a 100 hour.

Walt takes his glasses off. Correct. Abby's paid, but she isn't providing the airplane. You are, as an owner. So the law says annual only. I wrote the 100 hour into the agreement in 2009, because four people fly this thing and Abby teaches in it, and I don't like finding out about things at the annual. He hands the pad back. Good question to circle.

Tuesday came in gray and damp. It had rained overnight and the ramp was still dark with it, puddles in the tie down rings, the windsock limp. Biscuit had a new ELT battery, a new date in marker on the transmitter, a new line in the logbook in Marisol's capitals, and a fresh box drawn on the whiteboard.
A text from Abby Strand. 10 min out. Tower closes the north runway at 9 for paint, so we're on a clock. Be ready to start when I get there.
Jordan had the checklist in her hand. Marisol had been through every inch of this engine on Saturday. The oil was brand new. The cowling had been off and on and signed for.

Oil on the dipstick, the cap tight. Every cowling fastener. Static port clear, no tape. Fuel vent clear. Three cups of fuel, blue all the way down. It takes twenty two minutes and Abby waits for six of them, drinking coffee and saying nothing. Find anything? No. Good. That's what a preflight usually finds. You do it for the time it doesn't.

They took off on 35R and the door popped at rotation, like always. Jordan reached up and latched the top before Abby could open her mouth, and Abby snorted into the intercom. Out east the plains had gone green overnight, the air smooth and heavy as soup. The ATIS said thirteen degrees Celsius, dewpoint ten. She'd written that on her kneeboard right next to the strip of blue tape.

Abby had her fly a long slow descent at low power, 7,500 down to 6,500, then level off. Jordan pushed the throttle in. The RPM came up about halfway and quit coming. Then Biscuit started to shake, an ugly lopsided shudder through the floor and up into the yoke, a washing machine with one wet towel in it.
For one bad second all she could think about was the phone call from Claire in March.
Abby didn't touch anything. Your airplane. Talk to me.

She pulls the knob all the way out. The RPM sags another hundred and the shaking gets worse, much worse, for maybe twenty seconds that feel like a week, and she keeps her hand off the knob and holds altitude because that's the only job she has. Then it smooths out, all at once, like somebody flipped a breaker, and the tach needle climbs. She breathes out. Carb ice, Abby says. In May. At thirteen degrees. Now you'll never forget it.

Abby wrote up the lesson in the briefing room, 1.4 dual, and in the remarks put CARB ICE RECOGNITION AND RECOVERY, which made it sound much calmer than it had been. Jordan said she'd be a minute and walked back out to Biscuit.

She sat in the left seat with the door open and took the green composition notebook out of her bag. She'd been reading it a few entries at a time, rationing it. She flipped forward to see if he'd ever written about this. He had.

Danny's logbook, a page from June, seven years ago. June 3. KAPA local, 1.2. Pretty morning, 64 and wet after a storm. Long descent to Front Range, throttle back, admiring the view like a tourist. Added power, engine ran like a blender full of gravel. Pulled carb heat. It got WORSE. Which the book says it does. Which I forgot for the three longest seconds of my life. Then smooth as butter. Ice. In June. In Colorado. Carb heat on before every power reduction from now on. Marisol says she told me so. Marisol has told me so about everything.

Jordan laughed out loud, alone in the airplane, and then had to sit for a second with her hand over her mouth. Same airplane, same descent, same blender. He'd been scared exactly the way she'd been scared, and he'd written it down so somebody would know.

Back in the hangar Marisol was on the stepladder at the whiteboard. Under Danny's block capitals she was writing a new list in her own small neat ones, every item Jordan had found in the logbooks, with dates and tach times. She hadn't erased a single letter of his. The ELT line had a box around it and a new date beside it.
You find anything else in there, you tell me first, she said without turning around. Before Walt. Before the chat. Before Russ, God help us.

Marisol climbed down, opened the lid of her big red toolbox, and stood looking into it for a while. Jordan could see the inside of the lid from where she was. Taped to it, between a torque chart and a faded photo of a Super Cub on skis, was a short piece of safety wire twisted into an ugly lumpy spiral. Under it, on masking tape, in Marisol's capitals: D. REYES 2017. DO NOT FLY.

My divorce was 2017, Marisol said. Bad one. I was in here every weekend because I didn't want to be at the house. And your brother started showing up Saturday mornings with two coffees, saying he wanted to learn to safety wire. Every Saturday for a year. He was terrible at it. Worst hands I ever saw on a grown man. He never got any better, and he never stopped coming. She touched the wire with one finger. Took me till about Christmas to figure out he wasn't there to learn anything.

Jordan hadn't known. Nobody in the family had known. Danny had told them about Moab and dirt strips and the time he saw a bald eagle off the wingtip. He'd never once mentioned a year of Saturdays sitting on a bucket in a hangar, being bad at something on purpose so a friend wouldn't be alone.

He made that board so I wouldn't have to keep the list in my head anymore, Marisol said. And I let him. And then he was gone and the list just stopped. She closed the toolbox lid gently. Something soft shifted inside, a padded bag of some kind, and she put her hand flat on the lid as if to keep it there. You don't read like him, you know. He never read anything. You read like somebody who'd have caught it.
Jordan drove home with the strip of blue tape still stuck to her kneeboard. On the seat beside her the phone buzzed once.
A text from Abby Strand. Thursday 7am if the weather plays nice. Check the TAF before you text me. If you don't know what a TAF is, that's next week.
